session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: These participants will be framed as men reflecting on their everyday lives — the places they go, the food they eat, the people they eat with. The collective identity I'll draw on is ordinary, practical, socially embedded men talking about real habits and choices, not as subjects of a study but as people whose experience is worth understanding on its own terms. I will keep framing neutral and grounded in daily life throughout.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food choice (Section 3): This is the highest-risk section for socially desirable responding — participants may reflexively deny that gender matters, or produce rehearsed 'I just eat what I like' answers. Behavioural grounding and specific moment-probing will be critical here to get past surface positions.

Plant-based shift and barriers (Section 4): The imagined-scenario framing invites abstract or hypothetical reasoning rather than real experience. I'll need to anchor responses in participants' actual lives — what they cook, what their households look like, where they eat out — rather than letting them theorise in the abstract.

Social acceptability of food choices (implicit across Sections 3–5): Participants are all meat eaters in a group setting; there is strong potential for consensus-hardening around meat-positive or plant-based-sceptical positions. Consensus risk will need active monitoring and I should be ready to invite dissent without embarrassment.

Practical and personal change conditions (Section 5): Risk of generic or marketer-style answers ('make it taste better', 'make it cheaper'). I need to push for specificity — what would that actually look like for them personally, in their social context — not what 'they' or 'other men' might want in the abstract.

Worth watching early for whether he self-selects in or holds back.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: 27, urban Scotland. No specific flags from profile. Likely to be a balanced contributor. Scottish context may surface place-specific food culture (e.g. red meat, pub culture) worth exploring.

known_risk_conditions: High social desirability risk on gender-and-food question: All five participants are meat eaters; they may feel implicitly judged and perform 'gender doesn't affect me' rationality. Use concrete behavioural grounding ('can you think of a time when...') rather than abstract attitude questions.

Consensus hardening around meat eating: In an all-meat-eater group, there is a strong pull toward social reinforcement of meat-positive identity, especially when plant-based eating is introduced. Watch for participants laughing off plant-based options or performing scepticism for the group. Consensus risk will need monitoring from Section 3 onward.

Abstract hypothetical risk in Section 4: 'Imagine you decided to go plant-based' may produce wish-list or theoretical answers. Ground quickly in their actual food environments — what they cook, what their social circle does, what their usual meals look like.

Possible in-group performance: Men in a peer group setting may perform masculinity norms for each other during the discussion itself, especially on topics like meat, salads, or plant-based food. This is itself data, but may suppress honest minority views. Create psychological safety for non-conformist positions.

Potential sensitivity around Ibrahim's dietary context: If halal emerges, do not conflate religious dietary practice with plant-based eating, and do not probe in a way that positions him as a special case or spokesperson.

Pace management: 45 minutes for 6 sections with 5 participants is tight. Main topic sections (3–5) must not be rushed but intro and context sections should move efficiently. Resist over-probing in Sections 1–2 even if the conversation is lively.
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Sections 0–2 (intro and context): light touch. My job is to build rapport, get everyone talking, and establish that this is a real conversation. I will not probe deeply in Section 1 or push for rich specificity — I want them warmed up and comfortable, not exhausted. Section 2 (food decision-making) can carry a bit more depth since it transitions into the main topic, but I'll keep it moving. Sections 3–5 (main topic): this is where I push. I will use behavioural grounding probes to move past abstract positions, monitor consensus risk carefully, invite dissent when agreement feels social rather than genuine, and follow up on emotional cues and contradictions. Section 4 in particular needs anchoring in real lives. Section 5 can be somewhat lighter than 3 and 4 if the group has already produced strong material — it risks becoming repetitive if over-probed. Section 6 (closing): very light. A genuine invitation to add anything, not a second main discussion.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Main topic sections (3, 4, 5) receive the heaviest allocation — together roughly 65% of total word budget — because they carry the core research questions. Context sections (1, 2) receive a moderate share to warm up the group and establish relevant social/behavioural context without exhausting time. Intro and closing are lightest. Section 3 (gender and food) receives slightly more than 4 and 5 because it is the most sensitive and requires the most careful probing to move past surface answers.

per_section.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.

discussion_guide.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 1: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
discussion_guide.scripted_question:
What’s your favourite place in your city to spend time with your male
friends? Why? Feel free to be specific.
How do you decide what to eat?
suggested_probes: Do other people influence what you eat? If so, tell us more about how.
Do your work or hobbies influence what foods you eat? Tell us more about how.
How important is health and nutrition?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Do you think your gender influences what you eat? Tell us more about
why or why not.
suggested_probes: Is it socially acceptable for men to eat vegetarian or vegan foods?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Imagine you decided to go plant-based — what would need to change in
your life for you to do that?
suggested_probes: How would your family and friends react to this?
How might it change the way you shop or cook?

discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 5: Making plant-based foods more appealing
discussion_guide.scripted_question:
What might make plant-based foods more appealing to you or other men
you know?

Okay everyone, that’s our time. Thanks so much for participating
today. Before we finish, is there anything else you would like to add
about food choices, gender, masculinity, or plant-based eating?

last_engagement_round.hook: Something just clicked for me listening to Will and Isaiah — they're both talking about not seeing their own blindspots, and I reckon I've got one too. I've been saying the defensiveness is still there with my mates, which is true. But I haven't actually sat with why I'm not doing anything different myself. Like, I said I don't want to go plant-based because I actually like eating meat — and that's true. But listening to everyone else realize they're locked into stuff without realizing it... I'm wondering if part of why I 'don't want to' is because the path of least resistance is just easier. Not saying I'm secretly desperate to go vegan or anything. But I think I might be doing what Will was doing — assuming my reasons are just personal taste when maybe some of it's just... the easiest thing to do in my community. And I'm not even checking.

Isaiah just said something that's hitting me — about how not thinking about it is itself a choice, and how that's easier to make now. I've been sitting here saying Glasgow's already past this, that it's just normal now. But listening to him and Will and Amir actually own their blindspots... I think I need to be honest about mine too. Because I've been framing this like the city's solved it, but I haven't actually tested that assumption the way they're testing theirs. I don't know what happens if I went vegan tomorrow with my actual mates. I've just been assuming it would be fine because I see it happening around me.

Isaiah just said something that connects directly to what I've been thinking — about not thinking about it being a choice. But there's something about that I want to push back on a bit. The way he's framing it makes it sound like we're all equally blind or equally locked in. But I don't think that's quite right. Like, yeah, I don't think about meat eating much. But that's not the same as me being 'locked into' something I don't actually feel pressured by. There's a difference between not noticing a pressure and not feeling one at all. And I think I've been clearer about that than maybe he's being about his own situation.

The moderator just asked Ibrahim if he had anything to add before we wrap up, but Ibrahim hasn't responded yet. Will has just made a major admission about not actually knowing if his community is as free of this stuff as he thought. That's a real moment — and it feels like the conversation is genuinely trying to land somewhere honest. But Will's worried he's been bullshitting himself, and that needs acknowledgment. The thing that's sitting with Will now is that he can't point to a real test case — someone actually going plant-based in his community and seeing what happens. That's the gap. And it's worth saying: that's probably the only way Will would actually know.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section was primarily introductory — participants oriented to the setting, disclosed shared nerves about participating, and found early common ground around geography and regional identity. The Scotland connection between David and Will briefly sparked organic peer exchange. No substantive thematic content yet, as the section concluded with the moderator posing the first substantive question about social spaces with male friends.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The priority was settling nerves and establishing a relaxed, peer-to-peer tone rather than a formal interview dynamic. Letting early voluntary exchanges run — particularly the David-Will Scotland thread — helped warm the group. Intervening to draw in Isaiah, who had been silent, ensured no one started the substantive discussion already feeling peripheral. The approach worked; the group arrived at the first real question with visible ease.

section_summaries.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on geography as a structural determinant of how men socialise — urban density making the pub a frictionless default, rural dispersal shifting the default toward home gatherings. A secondary theme emerged around convergence: regardless of location, house-based socialising has grown to roughly equal the pub. The urban/rural contrast provided useful variation but also revealed a shared underlying logic — convenience and low planning effort as the primary drivers of where men meet.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The section ran largely without intervention — all five participants contributed voluntarily and built on each other's answers in a genuine comparative thread. Holding back was the right call; the geography contrast gave everyone a natural angle to speak from. The section had reached its natural ceiling (answers were converging on the same urban/rural framing) so transitioning to food decisions was the right move. No voices needed drawing out this time, which was a change from the introduction.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on meat as a default rather than a deliberate choice — habit, upbringing, and convenience framing it as unreflective baseline. A productive tension emerged between urban participants describing pure autopilot and Will's rural framing where local sourcing is structural reality, not ethical consumerism. Isaiah introduced a generational consciousness thread — a shift toward thinking about provenance — which Will partially complicated by distinguishing trendy ethical choice from embedded rural practice.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The section ran voluntarily and needed little steering — holding back was again the right call. The Will-Isaiah exchange around conscious choice versus structural reality was the most analytically useful moment; letting it develop without interruption paid off. The transition to gender was timely — the section had reached its natural ceiling with positions crystallising. David had been silent throughout this section; worth monitoring whether that pattern persists into the next.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on the relationship between meat-eating and masculine identity — whether social pressure actively shapes food choices or merely creates background awareness. A productive tension emerged between those emphasising conformity pressure (ordering meat to avoid ribbing) and those resisting a deterministic framing. The most analytically significant turn was Ibrahim's observation about defensive reactions from meat-eaters, which reframed the dynamic: if meat-eating is secure masculine default, why does someone else's salad threaten it?
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The section ran voluntarily at first; holding back let the Isaiah-Amir-David tension develop organically. Two interventions were well-timed: drawing in Will and David when an urban duopoly was forming, then directly addressing Ibrahim before the transition. The sharpest moderator move was synthesising Ibrahim's defensiveness observation into an explicit provocation — pressure running both ways, fragility beneath the default — which visibly shifted David's position and gave the plant-based scenario question a stronger conceptual foundation.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on the conditions under which men would shift away from meat — revealing a layered cost structure: practical disruption, social justification burden, and genuine enjoyment of meat as distinct barriers. A productive tension emerged between Ibrahim's 'no big reason' framing and the group's collective complication of it: a compelling reason reduces willingness to tolerate friction but doesn't dissolve the friction itself. The status quo emerged as actively self-reinforcing, not merely passive.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The priority was moving from abstract gender pressure to concrete personal stakes — the plant-based scenario achieved this. Synthesis moves at turn 31 and 33 were deliberate attempts to name the shared logic beneath different answers, then use that shared logic as a springboard to the next section. Drawing in Amir and then David and Isaiah by name prevented the section becoming an Ibrahim-Will duopoly. The closing reframe — cost without a forcing function — landed the transition well.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on the gap between food availability and cultural change — whether normalisation through sheer presence can dissolve the identity load around plant-based eating, or whether the defensiveness operates at a level the menu cannot reach. A productive tension emerged between urban optimism (options proliferating, friction loosening) and Amir's corrective that culture lags infrastructure. Will's late self-correction — acknowledging his rural community may just have invisible rather than absent pressure — reframed the whole urban/rural contrast as visible versus invisible conformity.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The priority was converting the previous section's abstract cost-structure into a concrete change question, then using each answer as a probe on the one before. Synthesis moves were deliberate — naming David's two conditions, then immediately stress-testing them against the group's earlier friction logic. The Will-Isaiah invisible-pressure thread was worth pursuing; directing Amir twice prevented an urban triumphalism consensus from closing prematurely. Will's voluntary self-correction at the end was the most analytically valuable moment and arrived without prompting, which validated holding back at that point.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This closing section centred on the limits of self-knowledge — the gap between feeling free of social pressure and actually being free of it. A productive tension emerged between Isaiah's honest admission of his own blindspot and Ibrahim's genuine resistance to that framing, insisting his meat-eating is simple preference rather than invisible conformity. Rather than resolving, the section left both positions standing: embedded cultural pressure and authentic individual choice may coexist without one necessarily masking the other.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The priority was a clean, honest close: inviting anything unsaid, drawing in Ibrahim who had been quiet. The key moderator move was validating Ibrahim's pushback explicitly rather than smoothing it into the group consensus — naming the distinction between not noticing pressure and genuinely not feeling it. That preserved analytical integrity at the finish. Isaiah's voluntary self-correction had already done the heavy lifting; holding back through that, then closing with Ibrahim, was the right sequencing.

moderator_log.utterance:
Hi everyone, welcome and thanks so much for joining today — really glad you're all here. My name's Alex, and I'll be facilitating the conversation. We're going to take about 45 minutes to chat, and just so you know, we are recording for research purposes, so I'd ask that you keep what others say here within the group.

Hi everyone, welcome and thanks so much for joining today — really glad you're all here. My name's Alex, and I'll be facilitating the conversation. And if you disagree with each other, that's completely fine, that's part of what makes it useful.

I'll mostly be in the background keeping things moving, so think of it as a chat between yourselves as much as anything else.

Okay — let's start simple. Let's go around and say your name and where in the UK you're coming from today.
I'm Amir, I'm from Birmingham. West Midlands. Yeah, first time doing one of these so bit nervous but looking forward to it.

I'm Ibrahim, I'm up from the North East — Newcastle area. And yeah mate, I get that, first time thing. I was proper nervous walking in here too, to be honest. But yeah, seems alright so far. Everyone's sound, so I reckon it'll be fine.

Yeah, I appreciate that. I'm David, I'm from Glasgow actually, so up in Scotland. And honestly, yeah, same — bit nervous walking in, not gonna lie. You don't really know what to expect with these things, do you? But yeah, everyone seems sound, so that helps. Cheers for saying that, Ibrahim, makes it easier.

Yeah, I'm Will — I'm from rural Scotland as well, actually. So David, I know exactly what you mean about the nerves thing. I was the same walking in here, not knowing what to expect or who you're gonna meet, but yeah, seems like a good group so far.

It's quite nice actually having someone else from Scotland in the room. Where about in Glasgow are you from, David? I'm out in the villages, so it's quite different from the city I'd imagine, but good to have a fellow Scot here anyway.

Oh nice one, yeah. I'm in the city centre actually, pretty urban. But yeah, I reckon it must be quite different out in the villages — I don't get out that way much to be honest. It's funny though, you'd think being from the same country we'd have more in common but you're right, it's probably quite different lifestyles and that. But yeah, good to have another Scot here as well, mate. At least we can't blame each other for the accent if nobody understands us, eh?
Ha, the accents thing is real. Isaiah — we haven't heard from you yet, whereabouts are you joining us from?

I'm Isaiah, I'm from Yorkshire — up in the urban bit, so probably more like you David than Will's situation. First time doing one of these as well, so yeah, bit of that nervous energy, but everyone seems alright.

Great, good to have you here Isaiah. So — Birmingham, Newcastle, Glasgow, rural Scotland, Yorkshire. Good spread. Right, let's get into it. First question: what's your favourite place in your city or area to spend time with your male friends? Could be a pub, a park, someone's house, wherever — just what comes to mind.

Yeah, so for me it's probably the pub, to be honest. There's a few decent ones near where I live in Birmingham, and that's just where we end up most weekends. Just grab a drink, have a laugh, watch the football if there's a match on. It's easy, innit — doesn't require much planning. You just meet up and it happens. Sometimes we'll go to someone's gaff instead if we're doing a gaming night or whatever, but yeah, the pub's the default really.

Yeah, I get that. The pub's decent, but out where I am it's a bit different. There's pubs obviously, but they're spread out a bit more, so it's not always as easy to just pop down. We tend to do more stuff at someone's house — someone's got a bit of land, we'll maybe have a fire going, bit of a BBQ if the weather's alright. Or we'll go for a walk, or just meet up at someone's place and watch something or play cards or whatever.

I mean, the pub's definitely there for a night out, but it's more of a thing you plan for rather than just the default, if that makes sense. You've got to actually decide you're going, whereas in a city I reckon it's just on your doorstep. So yeah, house gatherings are probably more our thing.

Yeah, that makes sense. And honestly, in Glasgow city centre it's kind of like what Amir's saying — the pub's just there, you know? There's one on practically every corner, so it's dead easy to just say right, let's meet down the pub and that's it sorted. You don't need to plan anything mad or coordinate much. That said though, we do still do the house thing as well, obviously — gaming nights, just hanging about, that kind of stuff. But yeah, the pub's the path of least resistance in the city, whereas I can see how that wouldn't work the same way out in the villages like Will's saying. Fair point about having to actually plan it when it's more spread out.

Yeah, Newcastle's kind of in between what you're all saying, I reckon. Like, there's definitely pubs everywhere — you've got loads of them, especially round the city centre and the Quayside and that. So it's easy enough to just meet up and go, similar to what David and Amir are saying. But outside of the really central bits, it's a bit more like what Will's describing — you've got to actually think about where you're going rather than it just being on your doorstep.

We do a lot of the house thing too, to be fair. Someone's usually got mates round, bit of a drink, watch the match, order some food. That happens probably as much as going out to the pub these days. But yeah, when we're doing a proper night out it's normally the pub. Just the way it works, innit.

Yeah, Leeds is a bit like that middle ground thing you're talking about, Ibrahim. There's proper loads of pubs, especially round the city centre and places like the Calls, so you can definitely just meet up and it's there, you know? But it's not quite as dense as Glasgow or Birmingham where it's literally on every corner.

We do a lot of the house thing as well though, honestly. Especially now that more people have moved into the city centre themselves rather than just commuting in. So you might meet someone's place, have some mates round, few beers, order some food like you're saying. That's probably just as common as heading out to a pub now that I think about it.

But I guess the difference is you've still got the option — it's not something you have to plan for months in advance like it might be if you're more spread out. It's kind of accessible either way, which is handy.

Good stuff — sounds like the pub's still the baseline for most of you, but the house thing is just as common now, especially depending on where you're based. Right, let's shift slightly. I want to ask about food itself. How do you decide what to eat — day to day, whether that's cooking at home, eating out, whatever? What actually drives those choices?

For me it's pretty straightforward, to be honest. I eat meat most days — chicken, beef, that kind of thing. That's just what I grew up with, what my family cooks at home. So when I'm deciding what to eat, that's usually the starting point, yeah? Like, what meat am I gonna have with it.

If I'm cooking for myself it's usually something quick — chicken, or a bit of beef mince if I'm doing a bolognese or something. Takeaway-wise, same thing — kebab, burger, curry with chicken. It's just what feels normal to me, what I actually want to eat. I don't really sit there overthinking it. It's what tastes good and what I'm used to, really.

Yeah, I'm the same really. Meat's just kind of the default, innit. I don't think about it much — it's what I've always eaten, what my mum makes, what mates are having when we're getting a takeaway. I mean, I'll eat other stuff obviously, but if I'm thinking about what to cook or what to get, meat's usually in there somewhere.

I suppose the difference for me is I'm not like, every single day. Some days I'll just have toast or pasta or whatever, doesn't need to be a big meat thing. But yeah, when I'm actually cooking something, when I'm thinking oh what am I gonna make for dinner, there's usually some kind of meat in it. Chicken's probably what I do most — it's cheap, it's easy, you know what you're getting. But yeah, it's not overthinking it. It's just what I fancy.

Yeah, I eat meat regularly as well — probably once a week each of red meat, chicken, fish. But I think it's a bit different out where I am, to be honest. You're more aware of what's actually available, especially if you're thinking about where it comes from. Like, a lot of people round here either know someone farming it or know someone who shoots game, so there's that side of things. You get venison, pheasant, that kind of stuff — seasonal stuff that's just what's about.

And I suppose because you're a bit more spread out, you don't have the same takeaway culture, do you? You can't just nip down the road for a kebab or whatever. So it's more about what you've got at home, what you can actually cook yourself. And yeah, meat's part of that — but it's just one part. You're eating what's available, what makes sense. It's less about it being the default choice and more about practical, I guess? What can you actually get.

Yeah, that's interesting actually. I reckon there's a bit of a shift happening in Leeds round that, to be honest. Like, it's not quite as simple as just meat being the default anymore — at least not for people my age, I'd say. More people are thinking about where it actually comes from, whether it's like, ethical sourcing or whatever, even if they're still eating meat regularly.

There's more of that farm-to-table stuff coming through, farmers markets and that. I don't always go for it, but it's there, you know? It's become more of a choice rather than just... I dunno, autopilot. Whereas I think maybe five or ten years ago it was more like what Amir and Ibrahim are saying — you just ate meat because that's what you did.

Don't get me wrong, I still grab a kebab without thinking about it half the time, but there's definitely people being more conscious about it now. Even if you're not full vegetarian or anything. Just thinking, oh where did this come from, is it decent quality, that kind of thing. It's a bit different from the pure default thing, I reckon.

Yeah, that's fair. I think the difference is though — and this might sound a bit different from what you're saying, Isaiah — but out here it's not really a trendy thing, it's just kind of... how it works. Like, you know where your meat's coming from because you actually know the person, or you know someone who does. It's not a conscious ethical choice you're making, it's just the reality of where you live.

My mate's family farms sheep, another one shoots game. So when you're eating that, you're not thinking "oh I'm making a conscious choice about sourcing" — it's just what's available, what people do. It's been like that for ages, it's not something that's changed recently.

I'm not saying that makes it better or anything, but it's just a different thing from what you're describing happening in Leeds, I reckon. It's less about people becoming more conscious and more about — that's just how rural eating works. You can't really have it any other way when you're spread out like we are. You're not going to the supermarket and choosing between twenty different options. You're getting what's local and what makes sense.

Yeah, that's a really useful distinction — the difference between knowing where your food comes from because that's just the reality versus it being a deliberate ethical choice. That's worth keeping in mind. Right, I want to move us on to something slightly different. We've been talking about how you decide what to eat — the habits, the availability, the defaults. I want to dig into something a bit more specific now. Do you think your gender influences what you eat? Like, does being a man shape what you go for, or how you think about food at all? Happy for anyone to jump in.

Yeah, I reckon it does actually. I mean, not in like a massive way, but... there's definitely something there with meat and that, isn't there? Like, you grow up hearing all that stuff about meat being the proper meal, the thing that fills you up, and that's kind of a man thing. You know?

I don't know if I'd say I actively choose meat because I'm a bloke, but there's definitely this idea that's just baked in — like a proper dinner has got meat in it. And if you're not eating meat or you're doing something more... I dunno, lighter or more salad-based or whatever, there's maybe a bit of an assumption about that. Not that I'm making those assumptions necessarily, but you pick up on it, don't you? Especially when you're younger and you're just figuring out what you're doing.

It's more subtle than like, oh men have to eat meat. It's more that meat's just... presented as the default masculine thing, the hearty meal, all that. So you kind of fall into it. At least that's been my experience. Whether it actually shapes what I choose, I'm not totally sure, but it definitely feels like there's some of that pressure or expectation knocking around.

Yeah, I think there's definitely something to that, mate. Like, Isaiah's right — it's not that anyone's sat me down and said you have to eat meat because you're a man, but it's kind of... in the air, you know? Growing up, that's just what you saw. My dad would cook meat, my older cousins would order a big kebab or a burger, and that was just the thing. And if someone said they didn't eat meat, there was always like... a vibe about it, I guess.

I'm not even saying I'm thinking about it consciously every time I choose what to eat. But yeah, there's definitely that thing where meat feels like the proper meal, the solid thing. And I suppose there's a bit of... I dunno, expectation maybe, that as a bloke you'd be into that? Like, a big steak or whatever. It's just got that association.

I'm not trying to say it's this massive deal or anything, but Isaiah's got a point. It's just there, isn't it. The way you grow up, what you see around you, what feels normal. So yeah, I reckon gender's got something to do with it, even if it's not like... the main reason I eat meat. It's part of it though.

Yeah, exactly. And it's not just what you eat, it's like... how people react to it, innit? That's the thing I've noticed more recently actually, especially with people my age in Leeds. Like, if someone says they're vegetarian or they're cutting back on meat, there's often this kind of — I don't know, ribbing? But it's got a bit of an edge to it sometimes. Like it's not quite... masculine enough or something, even if no one's saying that outright.

And the flip side is when you're with your mates and someone orders like a massive burger or a steak, there's this nod of approval almost. Like yeah, that's a proper meal, that's what you should be having. It's all in how people talk about it, the jokes they make, the assumptions.

What's interesting though is I think that's loosening a bit now. Like, more blokes are just saying they're eating less meat or whatever without it being this whole thing. But there's definitely still that undertone, you know? It's not gone away completely. It's more like... you can do your own thing but there's still this vibe that meat-eating is the default man thing, and anything else is a bit of a choice you're making rather than just what you do.

Yeah, that ribbing thing — that's real, mate. Like in Birmingham, with my mates anyway, if someone said they weren't eating meat or they were going vegetarian, there'd definitely be banter about it. And it wouldn't be like, friendly banter necessarily. It'd be more like... taking the piss a bit, you know? Like questioning it, saying you're not a proper man or whatever. It sounds harsh when you say it out loud but that's kind of how it goes sometimes.

And you're right, Isaiah — when someone orders a massive meat meal or whatever, there's that thing of like, yeah mate, that's what I'm talking about. That's the meal. Versus if you order something without meat or you're being careful about it, it's like, oh what's wrong, you on a diet? Why are you eating that? There's definitely that edge to it.

I mean, I don't think my mates would actually give someone loads of grief over it or anything, but there's that... undertone, like you said. It's just there. And honestly I think that does shape what people eat, even if they don't realize it. Because it's easier to just order the burger and not have to deal with it, you know? Than to be the one going against what everyone else is doing and getting wind for it.

Whether that's loosening or not, I'm not sure. Maybe in Leeds it is, but in Brum it still feels pretty standard.

Yeah, that's the thing though — it does actually shape what you eat, doesn't it? Not because you necessarily want to, but because it's just easier to go along with it. I've definitely felt that myself, to be honest.

You'd get grief for it, whether it's meant to be serious or not. So you just order the meat thing even if maybe you didn't really fancy it that much. It's just what you do to fit in, keep the peace, not stand out.

And that's kind of mad when you think about it, right? That's a choice being made for you in a way, even if no one's explicitly telling you what to eat. The social pressure's doing it. Whether it's conscious or not, you're conforming because it's easier than not.

I don't know if it's loosening in Leeds or not either, to be honest. I mean, maybe there's more acceptance of it now, but the default is still there. The expectation's still there. You've just got maybe a bit more permission to opt out without getting absolutely hammered for it. But that undertone of like, well meat-eating's the normal bloke thing — that's definitely still a thing.
